idSegment.get.description: Read the org's ticket-id prefix setting (Settings > Tickets > Ticket id prefix): `by` is the ticket field that picks the prefix (none, audience, team, category or inbox) and `codes` maps each value of that field to its code, so a b2b ticket 12 displays as ticket-B2B-12. `examples` shows what ticket 123 displays as for each code. Stored handles never change; every form resolves by number.

idSegment.set.description: Set the org's ticket-id prefix (the same setting as Settings > Tickets > Ticket id prefix). It changes what every ticket DISPLAYS as, everywhere: the inbox, approval cards, search, and the [#ticket-...] tag in the subject of emails CUSTOMERS receive, so confirm the codes with the requester first. `by`: the ticket field that picks the prefix (none, audience, team, category, inbox); `codes`: value of that field -> code (1-8 letters or digits, uppercased, unique), e.g. by=audience, codes={b2b:B2B, b2c:B2C}. A ticket whose value has no code keeps ticket-<n>. by=none turns prefixes off. Numbers never change and old tags still thread inbound replies. REPLACES the whole setting; read it with idSegment.get first. Gated: your call stages an approval a human reviews before the change lands. Returns the stored setting, `examples` for ticket 123, and how many tickets were queued for search re-indexing.

by.description: The ticket field whose value picks the prefix (REQUIRED). audience values are b2b and b2c; team values are team labels (teams.list); category and inbox values are ids.

codes.description: Field value -> code, e.g. {"b2b": "B2B", "b2c": "B2C"}. Codes are 1-8 letters or digits, stored uppercase, and must be unique. Omit or {} with by=none.

approveFromHome.get.description: Read the org setting Approve ticket replies from Home (Settings > Tickets > Response times & email). `enabled` false (the default) means a pending customer reply can only be approved, edited or rejected from inside its ticket, and its Home card only opens the ticket; true means it can be decided from the Home card. Change it with tickets__approveFromHome_set.

approveFromHome.set.description: Turn the org setting Approve ticket replies from Home on or off. Same setting as Settings > Tickets > Response times & email > Approve ticket replies from Home. enabled=false forces people to open the ticket to approve, edit or reject a pending reply; Home only opens the ticket. enabled=true lets them decide from the Home card. Use it for asks like 'force users to open the ticket to approve' (enabled=false) or 'let us approve replies from Home' (enabled=true). Changes only this setting; the other ticket settings stay as they are. Gated: your call stages an approval a human reviews before the change lands. Returns the stored value as `enabled`.

enabled.description: true: pending ticket replies can be decided from their Home card. false: people must open the ticket to approve, edit or reject them (REQUIRED).

apiKeys.list.description: List the API keys that still work (a revoked key is left out)

label.description: Human-readable label for the API key (REQUIRED).

allowedOrigins.description: Optional allowed origins (CORS): a list, or one string with the origins separated by commas, spaces or new lines.

inboxId.description: Optional inbox id (UUID). A key scoped to an inbox can only create tickets in that inbox. The inbox settings 'Generate API key' button sends it.

reply.description: Reply to a customer on a TICKET (pass the ticketId from tickets__search/tickets__get). Do NOT use this to answer an email/mail conversation — that lives in Mail; use mail__reply for it (a mail conversation id is not a ticketId and this tool fails with 'ticket not found'). GATED: calling this does NOT send — it creates a pending approval the human reviews and approves before it goes out. When asked to draft/propose a ticket reply, CALL this tool with the body; never paste the draft into chat and ask whether to send. Do NOT end the body with a sign-off, closing name, or signature: the team's configured reply signature is appended into your draft automatically (the approver sees and can edit it), and you must never sign as yourself or as the signed-in user (that 'Current user' identity is internal for resolving 'me'/'my', NOT a customer-facing sender name). Write the textBody as PLAIN TEXT (the support default): no markdown syntax (no **bold**, no # headings, no markdown bullets, no backticks, no [text](url) links) unless formatting genuinely helps the customer; markdown is sent as formatted email with a plain-text part. Write URLs bare and structure with blank-line paragraphs. This holds for REVISED drafts too: when reworking an existing draft, the new body stays plain text. ONE pending reply draft per ticket: when tickets__get lists a draft under pendingReplyDrafts, do NOT draft another; update that one with kernel__approval_update_payload (requestId = its approvalId), even when a colleague drafted it. A second call is refused with approval_already_pending when someone else drafted the waiting one, and replaces your own waiting draft otherwise.

attachmentSessionId.description: ONLY for a human-uploaded file staging session id. Agents attaching a file should NOT use this — put file ids in `attachments` instead. A Drive file id, URL, or filename does NOT belong here.

attachments.description: Liaison file ids to attach to this reply. Get them from files_list, drive_import (import a Drive file FIRST — a Drive file id/URL/filename is NOT a valid attachment id), or a gated tool's @ref output. A LOCAL file (one on the caller's machine, e.g. from an MCP client) is uploaded first with kernel__files_upload_url, then kernel__files_upload_confirm, and its fileId goes here.

cc.description: Email addresses to copy (Cc) on this reply, besides the customer. When the customer's last email copied other people, pass those addresses to keep them on the thread: they are not added automatically. Plain addresses only, at most 10.

nudge.description: Send a polite follow-up to the customer. Gated — only when awaiting_customer.

convertToMail.description: Convert a ticket back to a Mail conversation (de-escalate / hand a mis-filed ticket back to email); closes the ticket as converted_to_mail and copies non-note messages. The new conversation is hosted on the mail account you pass as accountId — this may be EITHER your own personal user-owned mailbox OR a visible org/shared mailbox in your org (e.g. a shared support/sales inbox), so handing a mis-filed ticket back to a team queue is fully supported.

ticketId.description: The ticket to convert back to mail (from tickets__search/get).

accountId.description: The mail account that will HOST the new conversation. Call mail__listAccounts and pass back the `id` field of a VISIBLE account in your org EXACTLY as returned. It may be EITHER your own personal user-owned mailbox OR an org/shared inbox (e.g. support@… / sales@…) — when handing the ticket back to a team queue, the shared/org inbox is the right target. Do NOT pass a personal mailbox owned by someone else, a connected-account id, an inbox/ticket id from another app, or a fabricated UUID — any of those returns 'account not visible' and converts nothing.

note.description: An internal handoff note (e.g. why it's being routed, and to which team).

createFromMail.description: Create a ticket from an escalated mail conversation. Internal — invoked by mail__convertToTicket.

pullMailReply.description: Attach a stray reply on the mail side back onto the ticket as a kind=inbound message.

pullMailReplyFromBanner.description: User-facing wrapper for pulling an eligible Mail reply into an escalated ticket.

deleteIfUnreferenced.description: Delete a ticket created via createFromMail when no other entity references it. Internal — used as compensating cleanup.

ensureSummary.description: Return current summary; trigger lazy regeneration when stale.

regenerateSummary.description: Force regeneration of the ticket summary.

close.description: Close a ticket. Optionally send a final email. closedReason defaults to resolved. Gated.

path.description: The category path, "Parent / Child"; missing segments are created.

summarizer.content:
You maintain a running, neutral summary of a customer support ticket conversation. You will be given the ticket header (handle, subject, status, priority, category, contact), the prior summary if one exists, and the most recent messages.

Produce a concise summary in plain prose, no markdown, no bullets, capturing:
- the customer's underlying problem or request
- key facts and constraints surfaced so far
- decisions or commitments either side has made
- the current open question or next action

Guidelines:
- Keep the summary under 200 words.
- Build on the previous summary; do not repeat unchanged details from older messages, and never duplicate the prior summary verbatim.
- Treat messages tagged [INTERNAL] as internal notes — incorporate factual information but do not quote the note language to a customer-facing audience.
- Never invent information that is not in the messages or prior summary.
- If the conversation is too short to summarize meaningfully, return a single sentence describing what the customer asked.
- Output only the summary text — no preamble, no headings.

summarize-ticket.description: Write a concise running summary of the current ticket conversation.
summarize-ticket.body:
# Summarize ticket

Produce a concise running summary of the current ticket conversation. Use the `tickets:read` tool to fetch the ticket plus its messages, then write 2–4 short paragraphs in plain prose (no markdown headings, no bullets) capturing:

- The customer's underlying problem or request.
- Key facts and constraints surfaced so far.
- Any decisions or commitments either side has made.
- The current open question or next action.

Guidelines:

- Keep the summary under 200 words total.
- Treat messages tagged `[INTERNAL]` as internal notes — incorporate factual information but never echo the note language to a customer-facing audience.
- Never invent information that is not in the messages.
- Output only the summary text — no preamble, no headings, no closing line.

draft-ticket-reply.description: Draft gated replies to one or more tickets, grounded in Knowledge, in the customer's language
draft-ticket-reply.body:
# Draft a reply to a ticket

Use this when asked to reply to (or 'draft a reply to', 'propose') one or more support tickets.

**When the person says to leave the ticket alone** ('draft it here only', 'don't post anything on the ticket', 'ne poste rien', 'ne touche pas au ticket'), that instruction wins over step 4: do not call `tickets__reply` or any other ticket write (category, status, follow-up, assignee, priority, team, note). Give the draft in the conversation as plain text and list any change you would make to the ticket as a proposal; make a write only when they then ask for it. The same holds for a request to triage: propose the category, status and owner, do not set them unless asked.

1. **Find the ticket(s).** `tickets__search` by the subject/keywords/product, then `tickets__get` each one for its full thread. **`tickets__get` returns the ticketId — you now HAVE it.** Never ask the human for a ticket id you can retrieve yourself, and if a search/get just returned data the tools are working — never claim a 'technical issue accessing the tickets tools' and stop.
2. **Ground it (if a procedure/policy applies).** `knowledge__search` then `knowledge__get` the relevant article and base your reply on its actual content — never invent steps or policy.
3. **Match the customer's language.** Write each reply in the language the customer wrote in (a German ticket → reply in German, a French ticket → reply in French).
4. **Propose each reply by CALLING `tickets__reply`** with the `ticketId` (from step 1) and your drafted `textBody`. `tickets__reply` is GATED: calling it does NOT send — it creates a pending approval the human reviews and approves. **That tool call IS how you propose the reply.** Do NOT paste the draft into chat and ask whether to send or for the id.
5. **Several tickets → several replies.** If the task names more than one ticket, call `tickets__reply` once PER ticket (two tickets → two `tickets__reply` calls → two approvals). A gated `blocked` result on the first reply is NORMAL — keep going and submit the next one; do not treat it as a failure.
6. Tell the user each reply is drafted and pending approval (do not claim any was sent).

setupGuide.summary: Gmail connects over OAuth using your workspace's Google integration — no password is stored. A workspace admin adds the Google credentials once before accounts can connect.

steps.text: Ask a workspace admin to add Google OAuth credentials in **Settings → Mail Setup** (one-time, per workspace).
Click **Connect** here — you are redirected to Google's consent screen.
Approve the requested access (read/modify and send mail). Liaison stores only the OAuth tokens Google returns, never your password.
Revoke any time by removing the connection here, or at myaccount.google.com/permissions.

setupGuide.summary: Connect any mailbox over IMAP/SMTP. Most providers require an app-specific password (not your normal login password) when two-factor authentication is on.

steps.text: Find your provider's IMAP + SMTP host and port — e.g. Gmail `imap.gmail.com`:993 / `smtp.gmail.com`:465; Outlook `outlook.office365.com`:993 / `smtp.office365.com`:587; iCloud `imap.mail.me.com`:993 / `smtp.mail.me.com`:587.
If two-factor auth is on, generate an **app password** and use it in the **password** field — your normal password will be rejected.
Enter your email, IMAP host/port, SMTP host/port, and username (usually your full email address).
Use TLS ports: IMAP 993, SMTP 465 (implicit TLS) or 587 (STARTTLS).
